Where it began

Bradley James Haddin was born in Cowra on 23 October 1977. When he was 12 the family moved to Queanbeyan, and he learned his cricket with the local juniors there before joining the Australian National University club, where he was playing first grade by 16.

His professional career began with the ACT Comets in the 1997–98 one-day competition. Looking for a bigger stage, he moved to New South Wales in 1999–2000, keeping wicket and batting right-handed for the Blues.

The player

Few keepers have needed more patience. For years he was Australia's understudy to Adam Gilchrist, playing one-day internationals from 2001 but waiting in the wings for Tests. When the chance finally came, at Kingston, Jamaica, in May 2008, he became Australia's 400th Test cricketer.

He made the most of it. In 66 Tests from 2008 to 2015 he scored 3,266 runs at 32.99, with four hundreds, 18 fifties and a best of 169. Behind the stumps he held 262 catches and made eight stumpings. He was also part of Australia's World Cup-winning squads in 2007 and 2015.

What made him special

The Ashes brought out his best. He made 136 at the Gabba in the opening Test of the 2010–11 series, and in 2013 in England he took 29 dismissals, a new record for a keeper in one Test series, every one a catch. Back home that summer he was even better with the bat, hitting five fifties and a hundred in Adelaide, and his 493 runs were the most any Australian keeper had made in a series. He was vice-captain as Australia won the urn back in Perth.

His Test average settled in the low thirties, which tells only half the story: when the top order wobbled, he had a happy knack of making the wobble look unimportant.

Away from the middle

After leaving international cricket in 2015 he became an ambassador for the Sydney Cricket Ground alongside Steve Smith. He moved into coaching, first as Australia's fielding coach in 2018, then as an assistant to Trevor Bayliss at Sunrisers Hyderabad and later at Punjab Kings. In 2024 he was inducted into the ACT Sport Hall of Fame, a fine honour for the boy from Queanbeyan.

And finally

In November 2015 he went back to the ACT Comets for a Futures League game, his first match for them since the 1998–99 season, and made a hundred in his first innings, 104 from 100 balls. Some players return to their old club to pass on wisdom. Haddin returned to score runs.
